entry.title: More on managing context and trees in pi
entry.summary: Four of my own commands on top of pi's session tree — /branch, /compress, /branches and /handoff — and when I reach for each one.
entry.content:
Fifth part of the series. The fourth one covered what sits underneath the tree; this is what I have bolted on top. Four extension commands, three in ~/.pi/agent/extensions/branch.ts and one in handoff.ts, and all of them run on the same API any pi extension gets: ctx.navigateTree, ctx.newSession and generateBranchSummary.

/branch — jump back to the last branch point¶

It asks nothing. It waits for the agent to go idle, finds the last branch_summary on the active branch (or the root if there is none), summarizes what you are leaving and drops you right there.

/branch  →  navigateTree(last branch_summary, summarize: true)

It is /tree without opening the session navigator and without picking the spot: the edge is decided by the last summarized branch. I use it to start a different attempt without dragging the implementation noise of the previous one. If you are already at that edge it says so and does nothing.

/compress — close the session and open a new one with the summary¶

/compact summarizes inside the same file and the summary replaces the old messages in context. /compress does the same but starts a fresh session: the summary is the first message of a new file and the original stays where it was, ready to reopen with pi -r if you need it.

Before touching anything it tells you how much it is about to summarize, using the real context size, and then it calls generateBranchSummary, the same code pi uses when compacting. That brings output limits, retries, thinking level and the list of read and modified files without reimplementing any of it.

The new session is linked to the original through parentSession, which is what makes pi -r show it hanging under its parent:

The summary lands as its own message (branch-compressed), collapsed to one line and expandable, not as something I appear to have typed.

/branches — which summarized branches the session is carrying¶

It lists the branch_summary entries on the active branch with a preview, estimated tokens (four characters per token) and the share of the context window they take. It is the detail behind the 🌿 status in the footer, which is recalculated on navigation and at the end of every turn.

The point is the usual one: when you chain a few /end without noticing, see how much context you are spending on summaries instead of on work.

/handoff — turn the context into a prompt¶

/handoff <goal> is the one least related to the tree and the one I reach for most when the next piece is a different task. It rebuilds the branch respecting compactions — the compaction summary plus everything kept after it — and asks the model for a self-contained prompt with context, decisions, files touched and the task.

The result opens in the editor so you can fix it before sending:

Once you submit it, it creates the new session with parentSession and the prompt already in the editor. The difference with /compress is what each one takes with it: /compress takes a summary of what was done, /handoff hands you the map of what comes next.

Which one I use¶

  • /end — 90% of my tree usage, with the marker cycle from the fourth part.
  • /compress — when the session is done: summary, new file, original intact.
  • /branch — a different attempt inside the same session file.
  • /handoff — the next thing is another task and I want distilled context, not history.

None of them is core: all four are my own extensions, which is why I can change the rules without waiting for a release. The tree gives you the pieces; what you build with them is yours.

Source: pi extension docs — navigateTree, newSession and generateBranchSummary.

entry.title: Session trees in pi — /tree, /fork and /clone
entry.summary: What sits under pi's session tree: entries with id and parentId, /tree, /fork, /clone, branch summaries, and the marker plus /end loop I use to reset context every day.
entry.content:
Fourth part of the series on pi. In the second part /tree was just another bullet in a list of commands. This is what sits under the session tree and how I use it: branching inside the same file, when to move work out to a new session, and the marker plus /end loop I close work blocks with so I don't drag noise along.

A session is a file with a tree inside¶

No database, no index. Each session is a JSONL file under ~/.pi/agent/sessions/, grouped by working directory:

~/.pi/agent/sessions/--home-pcaro-src-anotaciones--/<id>.jsonl

The first line is the header, with version, id, timestamp and cwd. From there on, every line is an entry with its own id and a parentId pointing at the previous one. That is the whole tree.

{
  "type": "branch_summary",
  "id": "62224c4f",
  "parentId": "8e2ca4f2",
  "fromId": "8e2ca4f2",
  "timestamp": "2026-06-11T17:00:15.313Z",
  "summary": "The user explored a different conversation branch..."
}

The detail that matters: the model only gets the active branch, rebuilt from the last message (the leaf) back to the root. Branches you walk away from are not deleted, they stay in the file and cost no context.

[user] ─ [assistant] ─┬─ [user]                 ← leaf: active branch
                      │
                      └─ [branch_summary] ─ [user]   ← alternate branch

/tree: branch without leaving the file¶

/tree opens the session navigator. It had no keyboard shortcut by default, so I gave it one in ~/.pi/agent/keybindings.json:

{ "app.session.tree": "alt+shift+e" }

The flow: you select a user message and its text goes back into the editor. Edit it, send it, and that creates a new branch at that same point. If you select an assistant response instead, it continues from there with an empty editor.

On long sessions the session navigator fills up, so the filters are half the value:

  • ctrl+t — hide tool results
  • ctrl+u — only my messages
  • ctrl+l — only labelled entries
  • ctrl+a — everything
  • ctrl+o / shift+ctrl+o — cycle filters

And to find your way around: shift+l labels the selected entry, shift+t toggles its timestamps, alt+←/→ (or ctrl+←/→) folds a branch segment or jumps to the next one.

When I use it: to compare two implementations from the same starting point, and when the agent has wandered off and I'd rather go back to the message where I lost it than rebuild context in a clean session. The failed attempt stays there and I can return to it.

/fork and /clone: when the alternative is other work¶

  • /fork — a new session from an earlier user message.
  • /clone — copies the whole active branch into a new session.

Both write a new file with parentSessionId pointing at the original. From the CLI there is pi --fork <path|id>, which cannot be combined with --session, --continue, --resume or --no-session.

The rule I apply: if the alternative is another variant of the same work, I stay inside the file with /tree. If it is other work that will live for days, it gets its own session with /fork. Mixing two different tasks into one tree ends up with a session navigator nobody can read.

Walking away from a branch without losing it¶

When you leave a branch, pi offers to summarize it and attach that summary to the branch you enter. It gets stored as a branch_summary with two references: parentId (the point you continue from) and fromId (the last message of the branch you leave).

The text is generated by the model with the same template it uses for compaction: Goal, Constraints & Preferences, Progress, Key Decisions, Next Steps, plus the list of touched files when relevant. And it always starts the same way:

The user explored a different conversation branch before returning here.
Summary of that exploration:

## Goal
Fix memory leaks caused by store subscriptions with onMount
and no cleanup
...

That summary is why /tree is not just navigation: the work from the abandoned branch reaches the new one as useful context, without dragging the hundreds of messages that produced it.

What I do every day: marker and /end¶

This is 90% of my tree usage, and it is the part that does not ship with pi. With the pi-auto-trees extension the tree stops being something I touch by hand:

  • /prime [scope] — an orientation turn over a repo or folder, with an automatic marker afterwards.
  • /marker — a checkpoint at the current point, without an agent turn.
  • /end — summarizes what happened since the marker, navigates back to that point carrying the summary, and moves the marker forward.

There are variants I pick depending on the moment: /end git adds the commit that should be made, and /end <instruction> gives the summary a focus (say /end focus on API changes).

The config is a separate file, ~/.pi/agent/pi-auto-trees.json:

{
  "summary": {
    "enabled": true,
    "model": "opencode-go/gpt-5.6-luna",
    "thinking": "low"
  }
}

A lightweight model used only for summaries; if it is unavailable, pi tells you and falls back to the session model.

Markers live in the session branch, so navigating back to an earlier point restores them, and what gets persisted are ordinary label entries: you see them in /tree with the ctrl+l filter.

That is why I almost never open /tree: every /end takes me back to the starting point, carries the implementation noise away and leaves a labelled checkpoint behind. The tree stops being a graveyard of attempts and becomes the index of the work.

Before you go¶

The tree is not there to pile up attempts, it is there so you don't pay for the same context twice. If a branch won't be useful even summarized, don't open it.

In the third part I go through the rest of the extensions I use daily. And if you are starting from zero, the first part explains what pi is and how it differs from everything else.

Source: pi documentation — sessions, session format and compaction.
